title: Things to Do in Gwalior: The Fort, Jai Vilas Palace, Tansen & Ancient Temples
seoTitle: Things to Do in Gwalior: Fort, Palace & Music | Kudozz Club
description: Things to do in Gwalior: Gwalior Fort with Man Mandir Palace, Teli ka Mandir and the Sas-Bahu temples, the light and sound show, Gujari Mahal museum, the rock-cut Jain statues, Jai Vilas Palace and its chandeliers, Tansen's tomb and music festival, and the zero inscription.
dek: A city in northern Madhya Pradesh crowned by one of India's great hill forts, the home of the Scindias and of the legendary musician Tansen.
searchIntent: History and music lovers planning one or two days in Gwalior, often with Orchha and Datia.

intro: Gwalior, about 120 km south of Agra, grew around a sandstone plateau that has been fortified for well over a thousand years. The Mughal emperor Babur is said to have called the fort the pearl among the fortresses of Hind. From the 18th century, Gwalior was the seat of the Scindia dynasty of the Marathas, whose palace still dominates the new city.

The things to do in Gwalior centre on the fort, with its palaces, temples, museum and giant rock-cut Jain statues, and on the Scindias' Jai Vilas Palace. Gwalior is also a city of music: Tansen, the great singer at Akbar's court, is buried here, and UNESCO named Gwalior a Creative City of Music in 2023.
One or two days is enough. October to March is the best time; the Tansen Samaroh music festival is held in December.

items.name: See Man Mandir Palace
body: Man Mandir, built by Raja Man Singh Tomar in the late 15th century, is the fort's most striking palace, with outer walls decorated with bright blue, green and yellow tiles showing ducks, elephants and banana trees. Inside, circular underground chambers were used in summer and, later, as a prison by the Mughals.

image.alt: Man Mandir Palace on Gwalior Fort
image.caption: Man Mandir Palace

items.name: Visit Teli ka Mandir
body: Teli ka Mandir, from around the 8th or 9th century, is the tallest structure on the fort, with an unusual wagon-vaulted roof that blends North and South Indian styles. Its origins and name are debated.

items.name: See the Sas-Bahu temples
body: The Sas-Bahu temples, a pair of 11th-century Vishnu temples, have richly carved pillars, ceilings and doorways. The name is thought to come from Sahasrabahu, a form of Vishnu.

items.name: Watch the light and sound show
body: An evening light and sound show at Man Mandir narrates the fort's long history, with Hindi and English shows.

items.name: See the rock-cut Jain statues
body: Along the road up the fort's western side, Siddhachal caves hold huge statues of Jain Tirthankaras carved into the cliff in the 15th century, some over 15 metres high. The Gopachal group, on another side, has more figures.

items.name: Visit Gujari Mahal and the gurudwara
body: Gujari Mahal, built by Raja Man Singh for his queen Mrignayani, now houses the State Archaeological Museum with fine sculptures, including the Shalbhanjika figure. Gurudwara Data Bandi Chhod marks the release of the sixth Sikh Guru, Guru Hargobind, from imprisonment in the fort.

items.name: Tour Jai Vilas Palace
body: Jai Vilas Palace, built in 1874 by Jayajirao Scindia in a European style, is still partly the family's residence. The Jiwajirao Scindia Museum inside has a Durbar Hall with two of the largest chandeliers in the world, said to have been hung only after elephants tested the roof, and a silver model train that once carried drinks around the dining table.
The museum's rooms display Persian carpets, a Belgian cut-glass staircase, antique furniture and portraits, and a gallery on the Scindia family's role in Indian history.

items.name: Visit Tansen's tomb
body: Tansen, the legendary musician of Akbar's court, is buried in a garden next to the tomb of his teacher, the Sufi saint Mohammad Ghaus, whose own tomb has beautiful stone lattice screens. The Tansen Samaroh, one of India's oldest classical music festivals, is held here every December.

items.name: See the zero inscription
body: The small Chaturbhuj Temple on the fort, from the 9th century, bears an inscription with one of the earliest known uses of zero as a written numeral.

items.name: Visit the Sun Temple
body: The Sun Temple (Vivasvan Temple) in Morar is a modern temple modelled on Konark, with a quiet garden.

items.name: See Datia and Orchha
body: Datia, about 75 km away, has the seven-storey Datia Palace, built in the 17th century by the Bundela king Bir Singh Deo. Orchha, a little further, has more Bundela palaces and temples on the Betwa.

items.name: Visit the Chambal sanctuary
body: The National Chambal Sanctuary, north of Gwalior, protects gharials, crocodiles, river dolphins and many birds. Boat safaris run from points such as Deori.

items.name: October to March
body: Pleasant weather for the fort and palaces; the Tansen music festival is in December.

items.name: April to June
body: Very hot; visit the fort early and late.

items.name: July to September
body: Monsoon rains; the fort's surroundings turn green.

oneDay: Drive up to Gwalior Fort in the morning for Man Mandir, Teli ka Mandir, the Sas-Bahu temples and Gujari Mahal. Visit Jai Vilas Palace after lunch, see Tansen's tomb, and return to the fort for the evening light show.
tips: Gwalior has an airport and a major railway station on the Delhi–Mumbai line.
Hire a car or autorickshaw for the fort; it is large.
Carry water; there is little shade on the fort.
Book stays early if visiting during the Tansen festival.
Hire a licensed guide at the fort to understand the different palaces and temples.
